claims.statement: Droṇa tells Duryodhana that today he will fell a foremost great warrior of the Pāṇḍavas.
flags: The handoff and scholar review had this vow at c. v.13; the e-text places it at 7.32.12, with the array at 7.32.13.

claims.statement: Droṇa will form an array the gods themselves cannot break, provided Arjuna is drawn away by some means.
The Saṃśaptakas challenge Arjuna and draw him away to the south.
At the word of his eldest uncle, Yudhiṣṭhira, Abhimanyu breaks the hard-to-break cakravyūha in many places (anekadhā).
Having done a hard deed and slain warriors by the thousand, Abhimanyu, caught among six warriors, falls into the power of Duḥśāsana's son.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra calls Abhimanyu not yet come of age (aprāptayauvana) and a boy (bāla), struck down by many skilled in arms.
flags: The handoff lists śiśu under 7.32 as well; in the e-text śiśu appears at 7.34.26 and 7.48.32, not in 7.32.

claims.statement: The arrangement of the cakravyūha: kings and princes set around Duryodhana, Droṇa at the head of the army and Jayadratha, king of Sindhu, standing firm beside him. The adhyāya gives no count of rings.
Yudhiṣṭhira says only Abhimanyu, Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa or Pradyumna could break the cakravyūha; no fifth is found.

Yudhiṣṭhira asks Abhimanyu to break Droṇa's array; Abhimanyu agrees, says his father taught him how to break in but that he cannot get out if trouble comes; Yudhiṣṭhira promises they will follow him in.
flags: The e-text reads yudhā in 7.34.20; check against the printed volume (scholar review, item 1).

claims.statement: Abhimanyu says his father taught him the method of breaking the array, and that he cannot come out if calamity befalls him.

translation.en: My father taught me the method of breaking the array, but if any calamity befalls me I cannot come out.

claims.statement: Saṃjaya tells how Jayadratha held back the Pāṇḍavas who tried to follow Abhimanyu, retelling Śiva's boon to him.
Jayadratha, loosing a mass of arrows, fills the breach that Abhimanyu had torn in the array.
Weaponless, Abhimanyu takes up a chariot wheel and rushes at Droṇa.
The warriors around him cut the wheel to pieces.
As Abhimanyu rises, Duḥśāsana's son strikes him on the head with a mace and he falls; thus one was slain by many.
Slain by six great chariot-warriors led by Droṇa and Karṇa, he lies alone, and the voices in the sky hold that this was not dharma.

translation.en: One against six he lies slain; this, we hold, was not dharma.

flags: The scholar review placed this at c. v.22; the e-text has eko 'yaṃ nihataḥ śete at 7.48.21c.

claims.statement: Abhimanyu is called a mere boy (śiśuka), not yet come of age (aprāptayauvana), when he is killed.
Arjuna returns from the Saṃśaptakas, senses disaster and finds his son slain.
Arjuna vows that tomorrow he will kill Jayadratha.
Subhadrā bears Abhimanyu to Arjuna.
Abhimanyu learns the whole science of the bow, divine and human, from Arjuna.
After his penance, Śiva grants Jayadratha that he will hold back all the Pāṇḍavas in battle except Arjuna. The boon carries no limit of one day.
Within the epic, the unborn Aṣṭāvakra speaks from the womb to correct his father's recitation, and is cursed for it.
Arjuna accepts Uttarā, daughter of King Virāṭa of Matsya, as his daughter-in-law.
Abhimanyu's son Parikṣit is born dead, struck by Aśvatthāman's weapon, and Kṛṣṇa restores him to life (birth at 14.65.8, revival at 14.68.18–24 and 14.69.3).
